title: Programming Foundations for AI
learning_outcomes: Explain programming Foundations for AI and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.
Apply the central idea in programming Foundations for AI to a small example or select a suitable approach for a stated scenario.
Identify an important assumption, failure mode, risk, or limitation and describe how it should be checked.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study programming Foundations for AI within Mathematical and Computational Foundations. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Mathematical and computational ideas make model behavior easier to reason about. Start with small values, explicit assumptions, and readable calculations.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: A reproducible AI experiment needs readable code, controlled inputs, dependency tracking, and a record of assumptions. Separate data preparation, computation, evaluation, and reporting so changes can be tested independently.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what programming foundations for ai takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the output. 3. Run the small example, compare actual and expected output, then change one input or assumption and repeat. 4. Record what the example demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate about a real system.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the task definition and the inputs available. content_blocks.run_instructions: Copy the code into a local file named main.py and run `python main.py` with Python 3. Compare the printed output with the expected result documented here. This CodeLeaf content block is static; it does not execute the snippet in the browser and needs no external API key.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet or return to the small synthetic input, rerun it, and change one value at a time. Do not add real credentials, private user data, or untrusted code to the example.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: A reproducible AI experiment needs readable code, controlled inputs, dependency tracking, and a record of assumptions. Separate data preparation, computation, evaluation, and reporting so changes can be tested independently. Next, connect this lesson to its prerequisite or next lesson and carry the same habit forward: define success, test a representative case, inspect failures, and document limitations.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a tiny numeric example for programming foundations for ai. Write down the variables and units, show the calculation or reasoning step by step, and check the result with a second method or a hand-worked case.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.
Record a prediction and compare it with a reproducible result or a clearly stated manual trace.
Document at least one limitation, safety consideration, or evaluation requirement.
hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
